profile.name: National Football League Cheerleading
profile.tagline: Sideline dance squads energizing NFL games since 1954
profile.insight: In 1954, the Baltimore Colts pioneered NFL cheerleading, now performed by 25 of 32 teams, blending dance, acrobatics, and military tours.
profile.profile: NFL cheerleading began in 1954 with the Baltimore Colts and now includes 25 teams performing dance and acrobatic routines during games. Cheerleaders also engage in marketing, charity, and USO military tours. Male and transgender cheerleaders have joined since the late 1990s and 2020s, reflecting evolving inclusivity. The squads perform in part-time roles with rigorous training and public appearances. Competitions and Pro Bowl selections highlight elite performers.
profile.profile_long:
National Football League (NFL) cheerleading is a professional dance and performance tradition integral to American football culture, originating in 1954 when the Baltimore Colts became the first NFL team to have cheerleaders. Today, 25 of the 32 NFL franchises maintain cheerleading squads that perform on the sidelines during games, providing entertainment through a combination of dance, acrobatics, gymnastics, baton twirling, and music. These squads are part-time engagements, often comprising current or recent university students who balance cheerleading with other careers. Their responsibilities extend beyond game-day performances to include marketing activities such as paid appearances, photoshoots, and charity events.

Cheerleaders also serve as cultural ambassadors through participation in United Service Organizations (USO) tours, performing for United States Armed Forces overseas. Notably, in 1996, the San Francisco 49ers Cheerleaders performed in Bosnia during the Bosnian War, and in 2007, the Buffalo Bills sent a squad to Iraq. Armed Forces Entertainment's ProBlitz Tours, starting in 2019, further extend these outreach efforts globally.

While the majority of NFL teams have cheerleading squads, seven teams—Buffalo Bills, Chicago Bears, Cleveland Browns, Los Angeles Chargers, New York Giants, New York Jets, and Pittsburgh Steelers—do not currently have official cheerleaders. The New York Giants are unique in never having had an official squad. In response, unofficial cheerleading groups have formed since 2010 to support these teams locally, though they lack official NFL sanctioning and cannot perform at games or use team branding.

The inclusion of male cheerleaders began in 1998 with the Baltimore Ravens introducing male stuntmen. The Dallas Cowboys established the first co-ed dance team in 2009, the Rhythm & Blue Dancers, featuring hip-hop and tumbling. Since then, other teams like the Los Angeles Rams, New Orleans Saints, and Seattle Seahawks have incorporated male dancers. In 2022, Justine Lindsay became the first openly transgender NFL cheerleader with the Carolina TopCats, marking a milestone in inclusivity.

The NFL cheerleading community also hosts competitions, such as the 1979 Battle of the NFL Cheerleaders and the 2006 NFL Cheerleader Playoffs, testing athleticism and dance skills. The Pro Bowl Cheerleaders, formed in 1992, select one cheerleader from each team to perform collectively at the Pro Bowl, representing the highest recognition within the NFL cheerleading ranks.

Despite their visibility, NFL cheerleaders have faced criticism and legal challenges regarding sexism, exploitation, wage disputes, and workplace mistreatment, highlighted in documentaries like "A Woman's Work: The NFL's Cheerleader Problem." Nonetheless, cheerleaders remain a prominent part of NFL culture, contributing to team promotion, fan engagement, and advocacy for female empowerment and LGBT rights.

Overall, NFL cheerleading is a dynamic, evolving tradition combining athletic dance performance with community outreach and entertainment, reflecting broader social changes within professional sports.

sections.origins_and_history: The first NFL cheerleading squad was established in 1954 by the Baltimore Colts. Since then, cheerleading has become a staple of NFL games, with 25 of 32 teams currently maintaining squads. The New York Giants are the only franchise never to have had cheerleaders. Cheerleading roles are part-time and often filled by university students or recent graduates. Over time, the squads have expanded their roles to include marketing, charity, and USO military tours. Male cheerleaders were introduced starting in 1998, with co-ed teams emerging in 2009. The first openly transgender cheerleader joined in 2022.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Technique not described in sources. Performances combine dance, baton twirling, acrobatics, gymnastics, hip-hop, stunting, freestyle, and tumbling. Squads perform on sidelines and stages during games, with choreographed routines. Male cheerleaders often focus on stunts. Rhythm and tempo details are not specified. Beginners would start with basic dance and cheer movements under professional choreography.
sections.music_and_instruments: Not described in sources. Music accompanies cheerleading routines, likely featuring upbeat, rhythmic tracks suited for dance and stunts, but specific instruments or musical forms are not detailed.
sections.costume_and_setting: Cheerleaders wear uniforms representing their NFL teams, often including team colors and logos. Annual swimsuit or lingerie calendars are produced by many squads. Performances occur on NFL sidelines, halftime stages, and during USO tours. Unofficial squads wear non-branded costumes due to lack of NFL sanctioning.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Cheerleaders perform during NFL games to energize crowds and support teams. They also engage in marketing, charity events, and USO military tours overseas. The Pro Bowl Cheerleaders represent the highest honor, performing at the Pro Bowl. Cheerleading serves as a platform for female empowerment and LGBT advocacy within NFL culture.
sections.notable_figures: Glenn Welt was the first male to try out as an NFL cheerleader in 1978 but was barred from competing. The Dallas Cowboys' Rhythm & Blue Dancers, founded by Charlotte Jones and directed by Jenny Durbin Smith, were the first co-ed team in 2009. Justine Lindsay became the first openly transgender NFL cheerleader in 2022 with the Carolina TopCats.
sections.regional_variants: Not described in sources. Variations exist between official NFL teams and unofficial cheerleading squads supporting teams without official squads. Male and co-ed squads have emerged in recent decades.
sections.lineage: NFL cheerleading descends from general cheerleading traditions in American sports, beginning with the Baltimore Colts in 1954. It has evolved to include dance, acrobatics, and military entertainment, incorporating male and transgender performers over time.

claims.text: Twenty-five of the thirty-two National Football League (NFL) teams have cheerleading squads who perform on the sideline during games.
claims.quote: Twenty-five of the thirty-two National Football League (NFL) teams have cheerleading squads who perform on the sideline during games.

claims.text: In 1954, the Baltimore Colts became the first NFL team to have cheerleaders.
claims.quote: In 1954, the Baltimore Colts became the first NFL team to have cheerleaders.

claims.text: Cheerleading in the NFL is a part-time job with duties including cheering, marketing, paid appearances, photoshoots, and charity events.
claims.quote: Cheerleading in the NFL is a part-time job. In addition to their main duties of cheering during football games, cheerleaders may have other responsibilities related to marketing the team for which they cheer, such as paid appearances, photoshoots, and charity events.

claims.text: NFL cheerleaders perform for United States Armed Forces overseas through USO tours, combining dance, music, baton twirling, acrobatics, and gymnastics.
claims.quote: Teams send their variety show, an elite group of their best members, to perform combination shows of dance, music, baton twirling, acrobatics, gymnastics, and more.

claims.text: Male cheerleaders were introduced in the NFL starting with the Baltimore Ravens in 1998 and the Dallas Cowboys co-ed team in 2009.
claims.quote: In 1998 the Baltimore Ravens Cheerleaders were the first squad to start using male stuntmen. ... in 2009, the first male dancers were added to the National Football League by the Dallas Cowboys.

claims.text: Justine Lindsay became the first openly transgender NFL cheerleader in 2022 with the Carolina TopCats.
claims.quote: In March 2022, Justine Lindsay, a transgender woman, made the Carolina Topcats, becoming the first openly transgender person to cheer in the NFL.

claims.text: The Pro Bowl Cheerleaders were founded in 1992, selecting one cheerleader from each NFL team to perform at the Pro Bowl.
claims.quote: The Pro Bowl Cheerleaders were founded in 1992 ... one squad member from every NFL team is chosen to participate in the collective Pro Bowl cheerleading squad.

claims.text: Several NFL cheerleaders have sued teams over wage violations, mistreatment, and harassment, highlighted in the 2019 documentary 'A Woman's Work: The NFL's Cheerleader Problem.'
claims.quote: Several cheerleaders have sued their respective teams for violating minimum wage laws, mistreatment from management, exploitative rules and behaviors, sexual harassment, and groping.
